344.title: The flood (Genesis 7)
344.hook: the fountains of the deep break open, and God remembers Noah
344.tomorrow: The dove and the olive leaf
344.howItsDone: Some churches pray for those in trouble by name each week, and the first letter of Peter links the flood to baptism, so some churches read the story at the Easter Vigil and recall it in baptism prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ark, tevah, a box built on dry land. Your line: build anyway.

Go back to the very first page. Darkness on the face of the deep, waters everywhere. Then God divides them: a dome to hold the waters above, seas gathered so dry land can appear. Creation, in Genesis, is partly a story of water being given its place. Now, in chapter seven, the story runs that film backwards. The waters come back, up from below, down from above, and the dry land disappears, as if the world is being unmade. And floating on all of it, inside a wooden box, are Noah, his family, and the animals.
screen: `CREATION: WATER GIVEN ITS PLACE.` → `THE FILM RUNS BACKWARDS.` → `A BOX ON THE DEEP.`

segments.voice: Here's how the King James Bible tells it: "the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened." The deep from verse two of the Bible, and the waters above the dome from day nine, both let loose at once. Rain for forty days and forty nights. The waters rise over the mountains, and stay for a hundred and fifty days. Two small details are worth knowing. First, the animals. Two by two is the famous version. But chapter seven also tells Noah to take the clean animals, and the birds, by sevens. Both are in the text. Second, after everyone is inside, there's this: "and the LORD shut him in." Noah doesn't close the door. God does. Then the long wait, in the dark, with no land anywhere. And at the turn, the first verse of the next chapter: "And God remembered Noah." In Hebrew, zakhar, to remember. It doesn't mean God had forgotten. Here, God's remembering is the hinge. Right after it, a wind passes over the earth, like the Spirit over the waters at the start, and the waters begin to go down. Christians read the flood in different ways: some as a worldwide event, some as a regional flood remembered in a great story, some as a story whose truth is about God and people more than geology. Other ancient peoples told flood stories too. However it's read, the text turns on three words: God remembered Noah.

segments.voice: Think of someone who's in over their head right now, grief, illness, debt, a long dark wait with no land in sight, and picture them wherever they are this evening. Hold them in mind the way the story says God remembered Noah, a remembering that leads somewhere. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.
The flood. The waters of the first page let loose again, the world almost unmade, and in the middle, the turn: God remembered Noah.
Your line: god remembers. And after remembering, the waters go down. Day three hundred forty-four, done.

345.title: The dove and the olive leaf (Genesis 8:6–12)
345.hook: the raven doesn't return; the dove comes back with a leaf
345.howItsDone: The dove appears across Christian art as a sign of the Holy Spirit and of peace, and in the catacombs of Rome early Christians drew a dove with an olive branch on tombs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the flood: creation run backwards, and the turn when God remembered Noah. Your line: god remembers.

Before radar and satellites, sailors lost at sea sometimes carried birds on board. When they couldn't see land, they'd let one go and watch. If it circled and came back, there was no shore within reach. If it flew off in a straight line, they followed it. The ark has been floating for months. The rain has stopped, the waters are going down, and the box has come to rest on the mountains of Ararat. But there's one window, and all Noah can see through it is sky. So he does what those sailors did, and lets a bird go.
screen: `SAILORS LOST AT SEA, A BIRD ON BOARD.` → `THE ARK RESTS ON ARARAT.` → `NOAH OPENS THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: The first bird is a raven. In the King James Bible, it "went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth." It never comes back with news. Ravens can live on what they find, even in a drowned world. Then Noah sends a dove. She finds nowhere to rest her foot, and comes back. And there's a tender detail here: Noah puts out his hand, and takes her, and pulls her in. A man who hasn't said a word in the whole story, reaching out the window for a tired bird. He waits seven days. He sends her again. And this time: "And the dove came in to him in the evening; and, lo, in her mouth was an olive leaf pluckt off: so Noah knew that the waters were abated from off the earth." One leaf. Not a field, not dry ground under his feet. Just a single fresh leaf in a bird's beak. Olive trees are tough; they can come back from almost nothing. And that leaf is enough for Noah to know. Something is growing again out there. He waits seven more days, sends her one last time, and she doesn't come back at all. Which is good news too: she's found a home. In Hebrew, dove is yonah, the same as the prophet Jonah's name. And for Christians, the dove will return at the Jordan River, when the Spirit comes down on Jesus at his baptism like a dove. Centuries later, the dove with an olive branch became a picture of peace across the world. It started with one leaf at evening.

segments.voice: Think about the part of your life that still feels underwater, and don't look for dry land or the whole answer; look for a leaf. One small thing growing again: a better morning, a kind word, a bill paid, one honest conversation. If you pray, you can give thanks for it.
Yonah. The Hebrew word for dove, the same as the prophet Jonah's name: the bird that came back with one green leaf.
Your line: a leaf is enough. The whole thing doesn't have to be fixed yet. That's day three hundred forty-five.

346.title: The rainbow (Genesis 9:8–17)
346.hook: God hangs up his bow in the clouds: never again
346.howItsDone: Covenant runs through Christian teaching, from the promise to Noah to the new covenant Jesus names at the Last Supper, and churches recall the new covenant at communion, in Jesus' words over the cup.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yonah, the dove, and one olive leaf that said something was growing again. Your line: a leaf is enough.

When two old enemies make peace, there's often a gesture. Swords laid on a table. A flag lowered. Something you can see that says: this is over. Noah's family has stepped out of the ark onto a scrubbed, silent earth. Everything they knew is gone, and the next time a storm cloud rolls in, they might wonder. So God speaks, not only to Noah, but past him, to everything that breathes, and makes a gesture you can still see after a summer storm.
screen: `SWORDS LAID ON A TABLE.` → `A SCRUBBED, SILENT EARTH.` → `A GESTURE YOU CAN STILL SEE.`

segments.voice: Covenant, in Hebrew berit, is a binding promise between two parties, the kind of solemn agreement that holds a family, a nation or a marriage together. This one is unusual. Listen to who it's with: Noah, his sons, their children after them, and every living creature, the birds, the cattle, every beast of the earth. Not just people. Animals too. And listen to what it asks of them. Nothing. There are no conditions on this side of it. God simply binds himself: "neither shall there any more be a flood to destroy the earth." Then the sign, in the King James Bible: "I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth." The Hebrew word for rainbow, qeshet, is the ordinary word for a bow, the weapon, the kind a warrior draws. Some readers picture it this way: God hanging the war bow up in the sky, unstrung, pointed away from the earth. Then a question: who is the sign for? You'd think it's for people, to calm them down when the clouds come. But God says, I will look upon it, that I may remember the everlasting covenant. The rainbow is a token for the earth, and a reminder God sets for himself. The same word as the flood's turning point: God remembers. Christians have gone on to speak of other covenants in the Bible, with Abraham, at Sinai, and the new covenant at the Last Supper. They start here, with every living thing, and a bow hung in the clouds.

segments.voice: If you're near a window, look out at the sky; if not, picture the last sky you saw, and let your eyes rest on whatever color is in it. Then think of a promise someone keeps to you without asking anything back. If you pray, you can give thanks for promises kept.

347.title: Babel (Genesis 11:1–9)
347.hook: humans build a tower to make a name for themselves, and languages scatter
347.carry: no need to make a name
347.howItsDone: Some churches read the Babel story at Pentecost, alongside Acts 2, and some read the Pentecost lesson aloud in several languages at once.

segments.voice: Yesterday, covenant: a war bow hung up in the clouds, a promise to every living thing. Your line: never again.

A ribbon cutting, a light show, a name in giant letters at the top of a new tower, so everyone driving into the city knows who built it. Building high to be seen is an old idea. In Genesis, after the flood, people move east and settle on a plain in the land of Shinar. Some readers picture the stepped towers of baked brick, called ziggurats, whose ruins still stand in that part of the world. Everyone speaks one language. And they have a new technology, and a big idea.
screen: `A NAME IN LIGHTS ON A NEW TOWER.` → `A PLAIN IN THE LAND OF SHINAR.` → `ONE LANGUAGE, A BIG IDEA.`

segments.voice: The technology is brick. In the King James Bible: "they had brick for stone, and slime had they for morter." Slime is bitumen, tar. Fired bricks and tar: a way to build high. And the big idea, verse four: "let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth." Make us a name: that's the heart of it. Not a temple to honor God. A monument to themselves, so they'd never be scattered. And remember, after the flood, God had told Noah's family to fill the earth. They want to stay put, and be famous. Then comes a line with a smile in it: "And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower." A tower meant to reach heaven, and God has to come down to see it. From heaven, it's tiny. So God confuses their language, and they stop building, and they scatter. And the city gets its name. In Hebrew, Babel sounds like balal, to mix up, to confuse. The text is enjoying the pun: Babel, the name of the great city Babylon, is tied here to confusion. Some Christians read the story alongside Pentecost in the book of Acts, when the Spirit comes and people from many nations each hear the apostles in their own language. Babel scatters the languages; Pentecost gathers people without erasing them. And there's one more contrast, coming tomorrow: they wanted to make a name. Tomorrow, God offers to make one.

segments.voice: Notice where your day goes into making a name: the post, the reply-all, the story told so you come out well, with no judgment, just noticing. Then think of one good thing you could do where nobody would ever know it was you, like fixing something quietly, and picture walking away from it. If you pray, you can offer it to God.

348.title: Go (Genesis 12:1–9)
348.hook: at seventy-five, Abram is told to leave for a land he'll be shown
348.howItsDone: Christian tradition calls Abraham a father of faith, and his call to go is read at some commissioning services, when people are sent out to new work, a new place or a mission.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Babel, a tower so small God had to come down to see it. Your line: no need to make a name.

Seventy-five. By then, the furniture is where it is, the friends are the friends, the doctor knows your name. Abram is seventy-five, living in a city called Haran, with his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, and everything they own. Sarai, the text has already said, cannot have children. Up to now, Genesis has moved fast, whole generations in a verse. Now it slows down and zooms in on one old man, because God is about to speak to him, and the story turns on what he does next.
screen: `SEVENTY-FIVE, SETTLED IN HARAN.` → `GENESIS ZOOMS IN ON ONE MAN.` → `THEN GOD SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Here's how it begins in the King James Bible: "Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee." In Hebrew, the first words are lekh lekha: go, and a little extra word that can mean for yourself, or even to yourself. Some Jewish teachers read it as a journey outward that is also a journey inward. Notice the order of what he has to leave. Country, then relatives, then his father's house. Each one closer, each one harder. And notice what's missing: the destination. A land that I will show you. No map, no name. Then the promise, and remember Babel. The people of Babel said, let us make us a name. Here God says to Abram: I will make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing. What they tried to grab, Abram is given. And not just for himself: in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed. The blessing is meant to spill over. Then one plain sentence: "So Abram departed." And "Abram was seventy and five years old when he departed out of Haran." He goes. Along the way, he builds altars. Much later, the letter to the Hebrews sums it up: he went out, not knowing whither he went. Jews and Muslims honor Abraham too, as a father in faith. And Christians often call him that: the one who went, before he knew where.

Then ask a smaller question: what is just the first step? If you pray, you can ask for courage for that one step.

349.title: Lot chooses the plain (Genesis 13)
349.hook: Abram lets his nephew pick first, and Lot picks what looks best
349.howItsDone: Some Christians read Abram's choice as a picture of peacemaking and humility, and his words 'let there be no strife… for we be brethren' are quoted when families or churches work through disputes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, go, lekh lekha: Abram at seventy-five, leaving for a land he'd be shown. Your line: go, not knowing.

Two families share a vacation rental. There are two bedrooms: one with a sea view and a big bed, one by the laundry room with bunks. Somebody has to choose. Abram and his nephew Lot have a bigger version of that problem. They've both done well, with so many sheep, goats and cattle that the land can't feed them all, and their herdsmen have started quarreling. Abram is the older one, the head of the family. The choice is his to make. And he doesn't make it.
screen: `TWO BEDROOMS, ONE WITH A VIEW.` → `TOO MANY FLOCKS, QUARRELING HERDERS.` → `THE CHOICE IS ABRAM'S.`

segments.voice: Here's what Abram says, in the King James Bible: "Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee, and between my herdmen and thy herdmen; for we be brethren." We're family. Then: "Is not the whole land before thee? separate thyself, I pray thee, from me: if thou wilt take the left hand, then I will go to the right; or if thou depart to the right hand, then I will go to the left." The older man, the one with every right to choose first, hands the choice to the younger. And Lot looks. He "lifted up his eyes, and beheld all the plain of Jordan, that it was well watered every where." The text compares it to the garden of the LORD. Green, rich, easy: the obvious choice, and he takes it. The Hebrew word for that plain, kikkar, means something round: a circle of land, the same word used for a round loaf, and for a talent, that heavy round weight of silver from the parable. But then the text adds a quiet warning: Lot pitched his tent toward Sodom, and "the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the LORD exceedingly." Choosing by what looks best has a cost the eyes can't see yet. And Abram, left with the hill country? Right after Lot leaves, God tells him: lift up your eyes. Look north, south, east and west. All of it, to you and your children. Lot lifted his eyes and grabbed. Abram is told to lift his and receive. The text doesn't call Lot a villain; he's family, and he'll be rescued more than once. But it lets you see two ways of choosing.

Notice what you feel, relief, a twinge of loss, a little pride, and whether anything is actually at risk. If you pray, you can ask for an open hand.
Kikkar. The Hebrew word for the round, well-watered plain Lot chose at a glance, pitching his tent toward Sodom.
Your line: you choose first. An open hand has room to receive. Day three hundred forty-nine, done.

350.title: Melchizedek (Genesis 14:17–20)
350.hook: a mysterious priest-king brings out bread and wine and blesses Abram
350.howItsDone: Many Christians remember Melchizedek at communion: the Roman Canon of the Catholic Mass names his offering, and the letter to the Hebrews, read in many churches, calls Jesus a priest after his order.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kikkar, the round green plain Lot chose. Your line: you choose first. Today ends the week.

Lot's green plain didn't stay peaceful. Chapter fourteen is a war story: four kings against five, armies sweeping through the Jordan valley, and Lot carried off as a captive with everything he owns. Abram hears, gathers three hundred eighteen men from his own household, chases the raiders north by night, and brings Lot back, with the people and the goods. As he comes home, two kings come out to meet him. One is the king of Sodom, who wants to make a deal. The other comes out of nowhere, says almost nothing, and vanishes from the story.
screen: `FOUR KINGS AGAINST FIVE.` → `ABRAM BRINGS LOT BACK.` → `TWO KINGS COME OUT TO MEET HIM.`

segments.voice: Here he is, in the King James Bible: "And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God." A king, and a priest, both at once. Salem is usually taken to be an early name for Jerusalem, and in Hebrew it sounds like shalom, peace. His own name, Malki-tsedeq, means my king is righteousness. He blesses Abram: "Blessed be Abram of the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth." And Abram gives him a tenth of everything, the first tithe in the Bible. Then Melchizedek is gone. No parents named, no birth, no death, no other appearance in Genesis. That silence made him fascinating. A psalm, the hundred and tenth, speaks of a king who is "a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek." The letter to the Hebrews, centuries later, builds a long argument on him: a priest without father, without mother, who points ahead, it says, to Jesus, a priest of a different order. And the bread and wine? Many Christians, especially Catholic and Orthodox, have seen in them an early sign of the Lord's Supper; the oldest Roman Mass prayer still names Melchizedek's offering. Others read it more simply, as a royal welcome of food for tired soldiers. Both readings start with the same scene: a stranger from no tribe the story names, blessing Abram with a meal. That ends a week of water and fresh starts: the flood, a leaf, a bow in the clouds, a tower, a call to go, a choice, and now, bread and wine and blessing.
screen: `A KING AND A PRIEST AT ONCE.` · `SALEM AND SHALOM.` · `NO BIRTH, NO DEATH, GONE.` · `A PRIEST FOREVER, IN HEBREWS.` · then, large: `HE BROUGHT FORTH BREAD AND WINE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone coming back from a battle of their own, a long shift, a hard week, and picture them walking in the door, tired. Then picture what you could put in their hands: not a feast, just bread, soup or coffee, offered with a good word. If you pray, you can ask a blessing on them.
Melchizedek. King of Salem and priest of the most high God, who meets Abram with bread and wine and a blessing, and then disappears.
Your line: bread and wine and blessing. Plain food, a good word, and then he's gone. Three hundred fifty days now.
